consumedBy.note: Each `descriptor` is exactly an AssessmentItemDescriptor and carries no other key. Authoring evidence lives beside it under `authoring`, which no runtime reads. There is no answer key in this file and verify.mjs fails if a key-shaped field appears — see answer-key.json.

idiom.options: Four options, A-D, one unambiguously correct. Authored items use A-D; the three released items keep TEA's own letters and are mapped by reference in released-item-map.json.
idiom.distractors: Every distractor is a real misconception rather than filler, named in `authoring.distractors` with the misunderstanding it catches.
idiom.reading: Stems are written at the same bar as the module: a thirteen-year-old reads them without a dictionary, and no option is longer than the stem.

provenance.note: The boundary of the Coercive Acts: three real acts inside, one earlier tax outside. Distinguishing the 1774 Acts from the 1765 Stamp Act is the chronology point the lesson's sequencing teaches.

descriptor.stem: Which of these was NOT part of the Coercive Acts that Parliament passed in 1774?

options.text: Closing the port of Boston to trade
Ending the Massachusetts town meetings
A tax on newspapers and other printed paper
Quartering soldiers on the town

authoring.askedBy: the edge of what the four acts include, from outside it
authoring.distinctFrom: The released items ask how the colonists responded to the Acts. This asks what the Acts were, and hides the boundary: three options are real Coercive Acts and one is the 1765 Stamp Act, so a student who has fused 'the British taxed and punished us' into one blur picks the tax.

distractors.A: Inside — the Port Act, the most memorable of the four.

authoring.negativeStemNote: STAAR capitalises NOT in a negative stem; it is the only negative stem in the pool.

descriptor.stem: Which statement describes the people of Boston and their representation in 1765?

options.text: They elected members to Parliament but had no colonial assembly of their own.
They elected members to their own colonial assembly but no members to Parliament.
They elected members to both Parliament and their own colonial assembly.
They elected no representatives to any governing body.

authoring.askedBy: the fact the whole argument rests on
authoring.distinctFrom: The released DISCRIMINATION item asks why a resolution was adopted; this asks the plain fact underneath it. A student can pick the right reason from a quotation and still not know that Boston elected anything at all.

distractors.A: The reverse — a student who has heard 'no representation' and applied it to the wrong body.
distractors.D: Nothing — the over-reading of 'no representation' into 'no self-government', which is the misconception that makes the whole objection incoherent.

descriptor.stem: On the colonists' own argument, a tax laid on them would have been lawful only if it had been voted by —

options.text: Parliament, because it governed the whole British Empire
The royal governor, who was appointed by the King
No body at all, because the colonists held that taxation itself was unlawful
The Massachusetts assembly, whose members the colonists elected

authoring.askedBy: the line between an authority the colonists accepted and one they did not
authoring.distinctFrom: RECALL asks what Boston elected; this asks what follows from it. The concept is a claim about legitimate authority, and this is the only item in the pool that asks the student to point at the legitimate one rather than at the illegitimate one.

distractors.A: The Crown's own answer, stated fairly.
distractors.B: The governor — appointed rather than elected, the same error moved one office over.
distractors.C: The over-claim: that the objection was to paying rather than to who asked.

provenance.note: No released multiple-choice item on non-importation is servable (STAAR.2024.G8SS.37 is image-dependent), so the concept is carried by authored items.

descriptor.stem: The colonists could not fight Britain's navy or tax its trade. What did they do to press Parliament by economic means?

options.text: They agreed to stop importing British goods.
They raised an army to invade Canada.
They placed a tax on every British good landed at their ports.
They sent the tea back to England.

authoring.distinctFrom: BOUNDARY asks what the answer was NOT; this asks what it WAS. A student running a 'they fought back' heuristic passes neither.

distractors.B: War — the 28% error, and not an economic means.
distractors.C: Counter-taxation — the 37% error, a power the colonies did not have.
distractors.D: The wrong year's act — sending back tea is 1773, and it is not a boycott.

descriptor.stem: Which of these was NOT one of the ways the colonists resisted the Coercive Acts in 1774?

options.text: A boycott of British goods
A written petition to the King
A congress to coordinate the colonies
A declaration of war on Britain

authoring.askedBy: the edge of the lawful forms, from outside them
authoring.distinctFrom: RECALL names the boycott; this hides it among the real forms and asks which is the one the colonists did NOT take. The wrong answer is the war a student expects the story to reach.
authoring.negativeStemNote: A second negative stem in the pool, on a different concept from the first; the two never share a form.

provenance.note: Cause-and-effect diagram with a missing middle step, a standard STAAR Grade 8 Social Studies stimulus form.

descriptor.stem:
Parliament closes Boston's harbour (1774)  ->  ?  ->  the colonies together agree to stop importing British goods

Which event best completes this diagram?

options.text: Delegates from the colonies meet in a Continental Congress.
Colonists board the ships and destroy the tea.
Britain repeals all of its taxes on the colonies.
The colonies declare their independence from Britain.

authoring.askedBy: the step that turns a closed port into a coordinated boycott
authoring.distinctFrom: RECALL and BOUNDARY ask what the answer was and was not; this asks what connects the punishment to the boycott — the congress that coordinated it.

distractors.B: The tea, which is 1773 and before the closure, so the chain runs backwards.
distractors.C: A repeal that did not happen and would end the chain rather than continue it.
distractors.D: Independence, two years early and not what a 1774 congress agreed.
